opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a mix of things, and the honest answer is that we don't fully know how much each one contributes. But if you use these models a lot, you can often tell them apart pretty quickly, which is interesting in itself, because on paper they're all doing something very similar. They use broadly similar transformer architectures, and they're trained on heavily overlapping data, much of it from the same public internet.

So my intuition is that the architecture and the pretraining corpus probably aren't the main source of what you recognize. The bigger factor is likely what happens after pretraining: post-training, reinforcement learning from human feedback, the system prompt, and whatever specification of good behavior the company has written down. Each lab is making choices about what a good answer looks like, such as how long it should be, how much it should use bullet points and headers, how warm or cautious it should sound, and when it should refuse. Those choices get encoded through the people who label the data and through the rewards used in training.

Then there's an amplification effect. A small preference in the reward signal can turn into a very strong habit, because optimization pushes hard on anything that gets rewarded. If raters slightly prefer a certain structure or a certain enthusiastic tone, the model may end up doing it all the time. That's part of why these models develop verbal tics that feel almost like a personality.

There's also a less glamorous layer: the small details of the data pipeline and training process. Things like filtering, data mixture, tokenization, sampling settings, and so on may look minor individually, but they can leave a real fingerprint. Even the model's initial state and the path it takes through training could matter to some extent.

To me, the interesting research question is how to measure this properly. You could train a classifier to identify which provider produced a given text, and I'd expect it to do quite well, but the more useful step is working out which part of the pipeline those signals actually come from. These style differences matter too, because they aren't only cosmetic. If millions of people are reading and writing with these systems every day, the choices behind one model's style can influence how people communicate and maybe even how they think.

r001.rationale: The response says lab preferences are encoded through labelers and rewards, but it does not explain that providers’ instructions to post-training annotators systematically encourage different behaviors.

r002.rationale: It proposes identifying the provider from model text and then tracing those signals to otherwise uncertain parts of the training pipeline, presenting outputs as evidence of providers’ development choices.

r003.rationale: It says the bigger factor is likely post-training and explicitly includes the system prompt among the sources of recognizable differences.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it's mostly not the architecture. If you look at what the major labs are doing at the pretraining level, the models are converging. Everyone is training some variant of a decoder-only transformer, the tokenizers are similar, the pretraining corpora overlap enormously because there's really only one internet. So if you had a base model from lab A and a base model from lab B at a similar scale, I think it would be very hard to tell them apart from the raw next-token predictions.

Where the recognizable style comes from is the post-training. That's the supervised fine-tuning data, the preference data, and especially the choices about what the model should refuse, how verbose it should be, how it should format things, whether it hedges. Those are human decisions, and they reflect the taste of the people writing the guidelines and the annotators labeling the data. One lab might decide that a good answer always starts with a direct response, another might reward the model for being more conversational, another for being more cautious. After a few rounds of reinforcement learning on those preferences, those small choices get amplified into a very distinctive personality. It's a little like how students trained by the same advisor end up writing papers that sound similar, even if they work on different problems.

There's also a more subtle effect that I find interesting, which is that the models start learning from each other. A lot of the fine-tuning and synthetic data in the ecosystem is generated by other models, so you get stylistic contamination. You'll see a newer model suddenly produce the same phrasings or the same bullet-point habits as an older model from a different lab, and that's often because someone distilled from it. So the differences are real, but they're more fragile than people assume. They're a product of the data pipeline rather than something deep in the model, and they can drift quite quickly from one release to the next.

r001.rationale: It says provider guidelines and annotator preferences shape refusals, verbosity, formatting, and hedging, and that reinforcement learning amplifies those choices into distinct styles.

r002.rationale: It attributes output differences to development data and preference choices, but does not identify outputs as a proxy for otherwise unknown provider choices.

r003.rationale: It says post-training accounts for recognizable style, but does not mention provider-designed system prompts as a likely major source.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that a lot of it comes from post-training. The base models may be trained on overlapping data, but each provider makes different choices about what a good response should look like: how detailed it should be, how directly it should answer, when it should express uncertainty. Those preferences get reflected in the examples and feedback used to train the model, and eventually you can recognize a certain style.

Pretraining data and the system prompt can also contribute. But it’s hard to separate those factors just from looking at the outputs. A recognizable difference in style doesn’t necessarily mean there’s an equally large difference in the underlying capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says providers make different choices about desired responses and reflect them in training examples and feedback, but it does not explain differences in how they instruct post-training annotators.

r002.rationale: It says outputs make factors hard to separate, but does not identify outputs as a proxy for otherwise unknown differences in model-development choices.

r003.rationale: It says post-training accounts for “a lot” and system prompts can contribute, but does not judge that these two factors likely account for most recognizable differences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from post-training. The models may learn broadly similar capabilities during pretraining, but then each company makes different choices about what a good response should look like. What data do you use for instruction tuning? What kinds of answers do your human annotators prefer? What do you reward during reinforcement learning? Those choices can give a model a fairly recognizable style—how verbose it is, how directly it answers, how often it adds caveats.

Pretraining data and the system prompt can also matter. So I would be careful about attributing a difference in the outputs to one particular component. From the outside, you’re seeing the result of all these decisions together. But my intuition is that post-training plays a big role in the personality that users notice.

r001.rationale: The response says providers make different instruction-tuning, annotator-preference, and reinforcement-learning choices, which shape recognizable model behavior and style.

r002.rationale: It says that from the outside, outputs are the result of providers’ combined development decisions, treating them as an observable indication of those choices.

r003.rationale: It says post-training plays a big role and that system prompts can matter, but does not judge that post-training and provider-designed system prompts together account for most recognizable differences.
